newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Annan to tell Cyprus U.N. opposes new arms buying.
newsitem.headline: Annan to tell Cyprus U.N. opposes new arms buying.

text.p: United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he would stress the world body's opposition to all tension-building arms purchases at a meeting on Saturday with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.
The Cypriot government's decision to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles has stoked tensions between the Greek and Turkish communities on the divided island and their backers in Athens and Ankara.

"Our position is that one should refrain from bringing armaments into the region that will lead to an arms race and build up tension," Annan told a news conference at the World Economic Forum in the Swiss resort of Davos.

Annan, who will meet a number of world leaders at the conference, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, said that Cyprus had a "window of opportunity" this year to resolve its long-running internal conflict.
The problem would deepen in 1998 because of local elections and the possible start of talks on Cyrpus's adhesion to the European Union, he said.
"We think we have a window of opportunity in the early part of the year to really try and make a difference. If we do not push the process forward, next year becomes more complicated," he said.
Turkey has warned that it would take all steps needed to block the deployment of the missiles which the Cyrpiot government says will not be in place for at least 18 months.

Clerides told a news conference at Davos on Friday that he was ready to halt the purchase of the controversial missiles if Ankara reached agreement on the future of the island, which has been partitioned since Turkish troops invaded the north 20 years ago after a military coup in the south.

The U.N. special representative for Cyprus, Han Sung-joo of South Korea, is on the island for talks aimed at bridging the gap between the two sides and clearing the way for a meeting between Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Raul Denktash.

"We are hoping to initiate proximity talks and eventually have a face-to-tace meeting," Annan said, noting that both Britain and the U.S. were appointing special envoys to help in the search for a settlement.

Annan was also due to meet Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas on Saturday to discuss the dispute between Jakarta and Lisbon over the future of the former Portuguese colony of East Timor, annexed by Indonesia in 1976. The issue has cast a shadow over relations between Asia and the European Union.
But he offered no prospect of a quick breakthrough. "It is going to be a deliberate and slow process," he said.
